lead: A Turing machine's finite control can hold a small amount of information in the names of its states. Instead of writing a symbol on the tape, the machine moves to a state whose name records that symbol. This saves tape work for bounded memories, such as the last two input bits. It cannot replace the tape for unbounded counts. Only a few universities teach this as a separate programming technique; it is used when designing compact machines and in proofs that add finite memory to a controller.
prereq: You need: designing machines with state routines from 5.3.

sections.h3: States can be named for data

blocks.text: The finite control is the state-holding part of a Turing machine. A state is only a name, so the designer can put data into the name. To remember the last two input bits, use four states: q<sub>00</sub>, q<sub>01</sub>, q<sub>10</sub>, q<sub>11</sub>. The subscripts are the stored bits. No tape cell is written for this memory. The head reads a symbol, moves right, and changes to a state whose name includes the new symbol. This helps when memory is bounded. It is the same memory as a DFA state, now inside a Turing machine; the tape remains free for other work. The state name is data for the controller, not for the tape. For alphabet size m and k remembered symbols, the control needs mᵏ states (m to the power k) to store every combination. Two bits need 2² = 4 states. A state can also hold a tuple, such as q<sub>a,b,c</sub>, for several small facts. The gain is fewer tape moves and a shorter trace. It cannot grow with input.

sections.h3: How to program with state names

items: List the bounded facts to remember and the input alphabet.
Make one state for every tuple of facts; name it q<sub>tuple</sub>.
For q<sub>ab</sub> reading c, go to q<sub>bc</sub> and move right. The oldest bit drops and c enters.
Keep a separate start state for short inputs and a separate accept state. Do not make q<sub>01</sub> accepting, because the machine would halt before the end of the input.
At the blank symbol, go to accept only if the stored tuple is the required one; otherwise go to reject.
Count states as tuples plus start and accept. Test one accepted and one rejected string.

To mark two symbols, use states q<sub>0</sub>, q<sub>1</sub>, q<sub>2</sub> to count how many marks are done. On each needed symbol, write a mark and go to the next count. This count is bounded; three states cannot count 100 marks. The head movement is still one cell per step. This is a finite memory.

spec.aria: Above, the input 1101; below, the run q00, q01, q11, q10, q01 with each arrow labelled by the bit read, and an arrow from the last q01 on blank to accept.

examples.question: A Turing machine must accept strings over {0,1} ending in 01 by storing the last two bits in state names. The memory states are q00, q01, q10, q11. Trace input 1101. (a) How many memory states are used? (b) Does it accept? Answer 1 for accept, 0 for reject. The separate start state checks that the input has at least two bits, then enters q00; the trace starts at q00 after that check. Inputs shorter than two bits are rejected by the start state.
steps: Read q<sub>ab</sub> as: last two bits are a then b. The four memory states are q00, q01, q10, q11, so the count is 4.
Transition rule: q<sub>ab</sub> reading c goes to q<sub>bc</sub>. The head moves right.
Start at q00 after the length check. Read 1: old q00, new q01.
Read 1: q10 → q01. The input ends.
On blank, q01 goes to accept because the last two bits are 0,1. Accept value is 1.
examples.answer: The machine uses 4 memory states and accepts 1101, so the answer is (4, 1).
examples.check:
states = ["q00","q01","q10","q11"]
s = "1101"
q = "q00"
for c in s:
    q = "q" + q[2] + c
accepted = 1 if q == "q01" else 0
print(len(states))
print(accepted)

code.code: No program is needed; the state table is the computation.

traps: q<sub>01</sub> is memory, not a halting accept state; halting there accepts too early.
Finite states cannot store an unbounded count; use the tape for counts that grow with input.
The update is q<sub>ab</sub> on c to q<sub>bc</sub>, not q<sub>ac</sub>.
Remember to add start and accept states to the state count.
Do not confuse stored bits with tape symbols; the tape still contains the whole input.

quiz.q: What do the subscripts in q<sub>ab</sub> store?
quiz.a: The last two input symbols, a then b.

quiz.q: Why can state names replace some tape writes?
quiz.a: A finite state can encode a bounded tuple; the machine reads and changes state instead of writing a marker.

quiz.q: Trace input 1010 from q00 using q<sub>ab</sub> --c--> q<sub>bc</sub>. What is the final state?
quiz.a: q00 --1--> q01 --0--> q10 --1--> q01 --0--> q10. Final state q10; last two bits are 1,0.

quiz.q: Why can no finite number of states count arbitrary 0s?
quiz.a: The count can exceed any fixed number of states; a finite set cannot represent all integers n.

quiz.q: How many states are needed to remember the last 3 bits over {0,1}?
Why use a separate accept state instead of making q01 accepting?
quiz.a: A memory state may appear before the input ends; halting on it would accept a wrong string. Accept only at blank after checking.

quiz.q: Is state storage bounded or unbounded?

beyond: Not for the exam. State encoding appears in hardware controllers, protocol finite-state machines and compiler lexers, where a fixed set of flags fits in a register. Verification tools model control state as an enumeration and search reachable tuples. Search terms: finite-state machine state encoding, one-hot encoding, product automaton, symbolic model checking.
